analysis.investment_thesis: Dachepalli Publishers fails both Magic Formula screens — a 0.31% ROE implies negligible return on capital, and a P/E of 15.9 (earnings yield ~6.3%) is not cheap enough to compensate. This is the opposite of the Magic Formula ideal: a mediocre business at a full price.
key_strengths: High promoter holding (64.78%) signals skin in the game
key_risks: ROE of 0.31% indicates the business barely earns its cost of capital
Earnings yield ~6.3% is below my 12% attractiveness threshold
Tiny INR 75.5 Cr market cap in a structurally declining print industry
red_flags: ROE of 0.31% — effectively zero return on capital
Print & publication sector facing secular digital disruption
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The Magic Formula ranks companies on two axes: how cheap (earnings yield = EBIT/EV) and how good (ROIC). Dachepalli fails decisively on the quality axis — a ROE of just 0.31% means equity holders earn essentially nothing; ROIC is almost certainly in low single digits, far below my 20%+ threshold. A good business compounds capital at high rates; this one destroys it in real terms after inflation. On the cheapness axis, a P/E of 15.9 translates to a ~6.3% earnings yield, well below the 12% I look for. Paying an average multiple for a sub-par business is precisely the combination the Magic Formula is designed to avoid.

The structural backdrop compounds the problem — printing & publication is in secular decline as readership migrates digital, making it unlikely the poor ROIC is a cyclical trough. High promoter holding is a mild positive, but it cannot salvage a business that earns next to nothing on its capital base. I would pass and redirect capital to names ranking in the top decile on both yield and ROIC.
